title: Global GTM Readiness Score
subtitle: Measures whether your startup has the customer insight, GTM motion, local network, and investor narrative to enter a new market.

questions.text: How precisely can you describe your ideal customer — not just the company type, but the specific person inside it with the budget and the burning problem?

answers.label: We have a broad target segment but have not gone deeper than industry and company size
We have named a job title and a pain point but have not validated it with real customers yet
We have a working ICP built from at least 5 to 10 real conversations
We have a sharp ICP with a specific role, trigger event, and budget range validated through closed deals
We have refined our ICP at least twice based on who actually buys versus who we thought would buy

questions.text: How many real customer interviews did you run before locking your current ICP and GTM approach?
questions.hint: Count actual phone or in-person conversations, not surveys or sign-up forms

questions.text: When your last potential customer said no, how clearly did you understand why — and did it change anything?

answers.label: We do not track lost deals or talk to customers who did not buy
We have a general sense but do not document reasons systematically
We debrief after losses but rarely change the pitch or ICP based on them
We interview lost or churned prospects and feed that back into our targeting
Lost deal analysis directly shapes which segments we pursue next

questions.text: How would you describe your competitive differentiation in the new market you are trying to enter?

answers.label: We are better, faster, or cheaper, but we have not tested whether that lands with local buyers
We have a positioning statement but have not stress-tested it with local prospects
We have spoken to 5 or more local buyers and have a working hypothesis
We have run competitive deals in the new market and know exactly where we win and lose
We have proof points specific to the new market: logos, metrics, or case studies from local deals

low.headline: You are still in the mirror room.
low.text: Building a GTM motion without knowing exactly who buys, and why, is the most expensive mistake a startup makes. This is fixable before you enter a new market.
steps: Run 10 real customer interviews with people who fit your target profile before your next GTM push
Ask every lost prospect one question: what would have to be true for you to have said yes
Write your ICP as a single named person, not a segment: job title, company size, the problem that is costing them sleep

mid.headline: You have a hypothesis. Now you need more reps.
mid.text: Your ICP work has started but it is not yet sharp enough to anchor a new market entry. Tighten it with more customer conversations before you commit resources.
steps: Push your interview count to 20 or more across your target market before scaling any channel
Document win and loss patterns in a simple tracker — you need to see the pattern, not just feel it
Test your differentiation claim with 3 local prospects before locking the pitch

high.headline: Your market clarity is an asset. Protect it as you scale.
high.text: You have done the customer work that most startups skip. The risk now is assuming the ICP that works in one market transfers cleanly to another.
steps: Run a fresh round of 5 to 10 interviews in each new market before assuming your ICP travels
Document your differentiation proof points market by market — what closes in Korea may not close in the UAE
Build a one-page competitive map for each new geography you are entering

questions.text: What is your current monthly revenue in USD?
questions.hint: Enter 0 if pre-revenue. Used to calculate your GTM efficiency ratio.

questions.text: How many hours per month does your founding team spend on GTM activities — outreach, demos, pitches, and marketing combined?
questions.hint: Include all founders' time combined. Used to calculate your revenue per GTM hour.

questions.text: How repeatable is your current sales motion — could a new hire run the same playbook and get similar results within 90 days?

answers.label: It is entirely relationship-driven and lives in the founder's head
We have some scripts and decks but the founder still closes everything personally
We have a documented process a new hire could follow, but it has not been tested with a real hire
We have onboarded at least one non-founder seller who is closing deals from the playbook
Two or more non-founders consistently close deals from a documented, tested playbook

questions.text: Where does your best new business actually come from right now?

answers.label: We are not sure — deals come from different places and we have not tracked the source
Mostly the founder's personal network, nothing scalable yet
We have one channel producing results but have not invested in making it repeatable
We have one clear primary channel and are actively scaling it
We have a primary channel working at scale and a second one in active testing

low.headline: Your GTM is founder-dependent. That caps your ceiling.
low.text: If only the founder can close deals and you cannot say which channel is working, entering a new market multiplies the problem. Fix the motion at home first.
steps: Track where your last 10 deals came from before spending another dollar on a new channel
Write down the 5-step process you actually use to close a deal — get it out of your head and into a document
Pick one channel, commit to it for 90 days, and measure it before adding another

mid.headline: You have early signals. Now make them repeatable.
mid.text: Something is working but it is not documented or scalable. A new market will require handing this motion to someone else — write it down now.
steps: Document your current sales process step by step, including what you actually say in each conversation
Run a 90-day test with one non-founder seller using only the written playbook
Define what a working channel looks like in numbers: specific lead volume, conversion rate, CAC — before calling it proven

high.headline: Your motion is scalable. Now check whether it travels.
high.text: A repeatable GTM is the hardest thing to build and you have it. The question is whether the same motion works in a market with different buyer behavior.
steps: Run 10 deals in the new market using your existing playbook before modifying it — learn what breaks first
Check whether your primary channel has the same reach in the new geography: LinkedIn penetration, event culture, and relationship norms all differ
Hire a local GTM lead who knows the buyer — your playbook is the starting point, not the final answer

questions.text: How did you decide which market to expand into next?

answers.label: It felt like the right move or we received one inbound inquiry from there
We looked at market size and picked the largest opportunity
We researched market size, competitive density, and buyer culture before deciding
We validated the choice by running initial conversations with local prospects and partners
We ran a structured market analysis and have closed at least one pilot deal in the target market

questions.text: What is your current network depth in the market you are trying to enter?

answers.label: We know almost no one there — we would be starting from zero
We have a few LinkedIn connections but no real relationships
We have 2 to 3 warm contacts who could make introductions
We have a local partner, advisor, or champion who knows the buyers
We have an active local partner with existing client relationships in our target segment

questions.text: How ready is your messaging, pricing, and proposal for a buyer in the new market?

answers.label: We plan to use exactly what we use at home — no changes
We would translate the language but keep everything else the same
We have adapted our pitch based on a few local conversations
We have run at least 3 real sales conversations in the market and adjusted based on objections
We have closed deals in the market and have a localized playbook with local proof points

low.headline: Entering a new market without local intelligence is expensive.
low.text: Most startups that fail at market entry did not fail because the market was wrong. They failed because they brought a home-market playbook to a place with completely different buyer behavior.
steps: Before committing budget, run 10 customer conversations in the target market — remote calls count
Find one local advisor or partner who has sold to your buyer profile in that market
Map the top 3 differences in buyer culture, decision process, and relationship expectations before you enter

mid.headline: You have a starting point. Now build the local layer.
mid.text: You know the market well enough to start, but you are still missing the local network and proof points that make a new market efficient to scale.
steps: Invest in one strong local relationship before you invest in headcount — an advisor with the right network opens more doors faster
Run 5 more local sales conversations and document every objection — that is your localization brief
Check your pricing model against local norms — what is standard in North America may not work in Korea or the UAE

high.headline: You are ready to move fast. Set a 90-day milestone.
high.text: You have the local intelligence and relationships to move quickly. The risk now is that early traction in a new market creates overconfidence before the motion is actually proven.
steps: Set a hard milestone for the first 90 days: a specific number of meetings, pilots, or signed deals — not just progress
Track local CAC and sales cycle length separately from your home market — they will differ
Plan your first local hire before you think you need them — strong local GTM talent has long lead times

questions.text: If a relevant VC asked to see your pitch deck tomorrow, how would you rate what you would send?

answers.label: We do not have one ready — it would take at least a week to put something together
We have a deck but it has not been reviewed by anyone outside our team
We have a deck we have used in a few investor conversations with mixed results
We have a deck that has generated meetings and we have refined it based on real investor feedback
We have a deck with clear traction metrics and are actively managing an investor pipeline

questions.text: How well do you know the investors most likely to fund your next round?

answers.label: We would start from scratch — cold outreach to a list we have not built yet
We follow some relevant VCs on LinkedIn but have no real relationships
We have a short list of target funds but only weak connections to 1 or 2 of them
We have warm intros lined up to 5 or more relevant investors through our advisor or founder network
Multiple investors have already expressed interest or we are receiving inbound from relevant funds

questions.text: How clearly can you tell the story of why your startup wins in your target market — specifically for an international investor who does not know your home market?

answers.label: We have only pitched to local investors who already know the market context
We have a general pitch but have not adapted it for investors from a different market
We have a version of the pitch that contextualizes the market opportunity for international audiences
We have pitched to international investors and incorporated their specific feedback
We have closed international investors or have strong LOIs from funds outside our home market

low.headline: Your fundraising narrative is not ready for a global audience.
low.text: International VCs do not have the local context you assume. If your pitch depends on investors already knowing your market, you are cutting yourself off from most of the capital available to you.
steps: Review 5 pitch decks from a16z or YC portfolio companies in your category — notice how they contextualize their market for a global reader
Build your investor shortlist now, before you are in the market — sourcing takes 3 times longer than founders expect
Find one advisor who has raised from international investors in your sector and run your pitch by them

mid.headline: You have a fundable story. Now build the relationships before you need them.
mid.text: The founders who close rounds quickly already had the investor relationships in place. The deck is secondary.
steps: Map your path to warm intros for your top 20 target investors — LinkedIn connections and advisor networks both count
Get one external review of your deck from a founder who has raised from international VCs
Practice your international pitch with 5 people who have no context on your home market — their confusion is your feedback

high.headline: You are in a strong position. Protect your momentum.
high.text: You have the narrative, the network, and the traction story. The risk now is process — fundraising without a clear timeline and investor management system turns into a distraction.
steps: Set a hard close date for your round and work backwards from it to manage your investor pipeline
Dedicate one founder to fundraising full-time — mixing GTM and fundraising dilutes both
Keep building your investor relationship log between rounds — the best fundraises start 12 months before the ask

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.

persona_selector.text: Which best describes you right now?

answers.label: Founder running GTM myself
GTM or sales leader at a startup
Startup team member contributing to growth
Investor or advisor evaluating a startup's GTM
